rationale: Pes cavus and associated foot deformities (such as hammer toes and hallux valgus) are repeatedly reported in patients with heterozygous loss-of-function variants in SPTAN1 (dHMN11), including reports by Dong et al. (2021), Beijer et al. (2019), and Van de Vondel et al. (2026). However, the hypothesis that pes cavus specifically occurs in 50% to 100% of symptomatic individuals and acts unequivocally as a physical hallmark of lower limb denervation is conflicted. First, phenotypic spectrum analysis reveals variable penetrance and variable manifestations (ranging from hallux valgus alone to severe pes cavus and hammer toes). Second, recent literature demonstrates that heterozygous SPTAN1 loss-of-function and deletions can present primarily with a distal myopathy rather than classical neurogenic denervation/dHMN, with myopathic EMG and muscle biopsy findings causing frequent diagnostic confusion.

evidence.text: Dong et al. (2021) identified a de novo nonsense mutation in SPTAN1 in a Chinese proband presenting with distal hereditary motor neuropathy, claw hands, and pes cavus noted on neurological examination at age 21.

conflicts: Foot deformities in heterozygous SPTAN1 loss-of-function cases are heterogeneous: while pes cavus and hammer toes are common, some symptomatic individuals display hallux valgus without overt pes cavus, and variable penetrance exists.

Pes cavus and distal weakness in patients with SPTAN1 loss-of-function variants do not uniquely reflect lower motor neuron denervation, as multiple cohorts demonstrate these same features arising secondary to primary distal myopathy.

new_directions.question_text: What is the exact incidence of isolated pes cavus versus other foot deformities across all molecularly confirmed SPTAN1 haploinsufficiency cases after stratifying by neurogenic versus primary myopathic EMG patterns?
new_directions.rationale: Clarifying the electrophysiological and histopathological etiology will determine whether foot deformities are neurogenic, myogenic, or secondary to intrinsic biomechanical foot muscle imbalances.

new_directions.question_text: Does lower limb muscle MRI fat replacement patterning reliably distinguish SPTAN1-associated dHMN from SPTAN1-associated distal myopathy in juvenile patients presenting with pes cavus?
new_directions.rationale: Dohrn & Saporta (2020) demonstrated distinct MRI signatures (reticular vs moth-eaten fat replacement) between dHMN and distal myopathies, which could resolve diagnostic ambiguities.
